options: Waits up to 1 second for new records and returns a batch of whatever's available, possibly empty
Blocks forever until at least one record arrives, with no way to return early
Deletes the topic after 1 second if no consumer has read it
Commits the consumer's offset automatically every 1 second regardless of processing
questions.explain: The timeout controls how long to wait for something to become available, not a hard limit on how long processing may take.

options: Only when there's no prior committed offset to resume from — once committed, a consumer always resumes from that position
On every single poll() call, regardless of committed offsets
Only for producers, never for consumers
It controls how many partitions a topic has
questions.explain: auto.offset.reset decides the starting point only the first time a group reads a topic, or if its committed offset has aged out of retention.

questions.q: Why does earliest fit a backfill or analytics pipeline better than latest?
options: Earliest starts from the very beginning of retained history, so no historical events are skipped
Earliest is always faster than latest regardless of use case
Earliest deletes old data as it reads it
Earliest and latest behave identically in every situation
questions.explain: A backfill or analytics workload typically needs the full historical picture, which earliest provides and latest skips.

questions.q: What's the real gap in relying on auto-commit?
options: If the consumer crashes after an auto-commit but before finishing that batch's processing, the batch is marked processed even though it wasn't
Auto-commit is not supported by any real Kafka client
Auto-commit always commits before poll() even returns any records
Auto-commit prevents a consumer from ever crashing
questions.explain: The timer-based commit doesn't know whether handle() actually finished, so a crash at the wrong moment silently loses that batch's work.

questions.q: What does committing manually, only after `handle()` succeeds, actually buy you?
options: It closes the gap where a crash could mark unfinished work as already processed — at the cost of writing the commit call yourself
It makes poll() return instantly with zero latency
It removes the need for a consumer group entirely
It guarantees exactly-once delivery with no other configuration required
questions.explain: Manual commit after real processing is exactly the pattern behind at-least-once delivery, which Lesson 9 builds on directly.
